CausalChain: Chronic inflammation -> Activation of CAFs -> ECM remodeling and increased stiffness -> Enhanced mechanotransduction (YAP/TAZ activation plus additional TGF-β signaling) -> Induction of partial EMT and CSC-like traits, along with immune evasion -> Increased chemoresistance and immunotherapy resistance
Hypothesis: In cholangiocarcinoma, chronic inflammatory signals induce CAF activation, which remodels and stiffens the ECM. This stiffened matrix, together with cytokine and growth factor signaling, activates YAP/TAZ as well as complementary mechanotransduction pathways (e.g., TGF-β) that drive a partial EMT and the emergence of cancer stem cell–like properties while concurrently establishing an immune-suppressive microenvironment. We propose that this integrated cascade underlies the development of both chemoresistance and immunotherapy resistance. By employing advanced 3D culture systems, precise biomechanical sensors, high-resolution imaging, and AI-powered data analysis to monitor ECM stiffness and YAP/TAZ dynamics, targeted combined therapeutic strategies that inhibit YAP/TAZ and its compensatory pathways can be developed. This multifaceted intervention holds promise for overcoming drug resistance in cholangiocarcinoma.
Abstract: Chronic inflammation in cholangiocarcinoma activates cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), triggering a cascade of extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling that increases tissue stiffness. This biomechanical alteration, in conjunction with inflammatory cytokines and growth factors, enhances mechanotransduction primarily via YAP/TAZ signaling as well as complementary pathways (such as TGF-β signaling). The integrated signaling network drives a partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and fosters cancer stem cell–like features, concurrently promoting immune evasion. Leveraging contemporary technologies—such as tunable 3D microfluidic culture systems, advanced imaging modalities, and AI-based analytics for real-time quantification of ECM stiffness and YAP/TAZ localization—this study posits that dual-targeted inhibition of YAP/TAZ and associated compensatory mechanisms can improve chemotherapeutic outcomes and reverse drug resistance in cholangiocarcinoma.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis centered on CAF-mediated ECM stiffening activating YAP/TAZ signaling, which in turn promoted EMT and CSC-like transformation leading to chemoresistance. The new hypothesis retains this fundamental causal chain but expands it by: (1) incorporating the role of additional cytokine and growth factor signaling (e.g., TGF-β) which may contribute to a more nuanced, partial EMT and modulate immune evasion; (2) acknowledging the possibility of redundant or compensatory mechanotransduction pathways; and (3) enhancing practical feasibly by integrating advanced technological platforms (3D microfluidic cultures, high-resolution imaging, and AI analytics) for precise quantification and targeted intervention. These revisions solidify the mechanistic understanding and broaden potential therapeutic strategies while aligning more closely with contemporary research and technological capabilities.
